item.title: 'I worked so hard' - Vatuwaqa resident loses home and vehicles in fire
item.description: It was not a good Sunday for Timoci Nadukena, whose home was destroyed in a fire at Muanivatu Settlement in Vatuwaqa this morning. Nadukena says he was at the Waila Market when a friend informed him that his house was on fire.
item.content:encoded:
It was not a good Sunday for Timoci Nadukena, whose home was destroyed in a fire at Muanivatu Settlement in Vatuwaqa this morning.

Nadukena says he was at the Waila Market when a friend informed him that his house was on fire.

He says he initially did not believe his friend, but soon realised he was serious.

When he arrived home, he found the house engulfed in flames.

Nadukena says his child was home alone when the fire broke out a nd noticed that the fire had started in the mother's room before running out of the house.

He is grateful that no one was injured, especially his child.

However, the fire destroyed all their belongings, including his two vehicles.

Nadukena says he has worked so hard to build what he had, only to lose it all in the fire.

He says he does not know what he will do next and is appealing to the Government to assist him and his family.

The cause of the fire is yet to be determined, and firefighters are at the scene.

We have sent questions to the National Fire Authority.

item.title: Constitution consultation process makes a mockery of democracy – NFP President
item.description: This constitutional consultation process is being rushed, and the manner in which it is being conducted is making a mockery of the principles of democracy. This has been highlighted by National Federation Party President Parmod Chand, who says the process is fundamentally unfair to the people of Fiji.
item.content:encoded:
This constitutional consultation process is being rushed, and the manner in which it is being conducted is making a mockery of the principles of democracy.

This has been highlighted by National Federation Party President Parmod Chand, who says the process is fundamentally unfair to the people of Fiji.

Chand says the people of Fiji are being given limited time to make submissions on a proposed Constitution that will determine their rights, the powers of institutions, land ownership and the foundations of democracy for generations.

Chand says people travelling from villages, settlements, farms and towns to appear before the Committee are being given only a limited number of minutes to speak, with some barely beginning to explain their concerns before being reminded of the time.

He says the Committee is expected to complete its work within 20 days, including consultations, preliminary work and the compilation of its report, while the public was initially given just 13 days to make submissions on the Government's Bill.

Chand is calling on the Committee to recommend an extension of public consultations until mid-December and ensure people are given adequate time to be heard, even if the process continues after the next elections.

He says the Constitution belongs to the people of Fiji, not Parliament or the Government, and no political timetable should dictate how much time people are permitted to spend discussing it.

Chand says if the Committee continues on its current path, it will be remembered for producing a Constitution that is fast-tracked and worse than the 2013 Constitution.

Chand adds that the Government has not published or broadcast the contents of the Bill in English, Vosa Vakaviti and Hindi, which he says is necessary to ensure all Fijians understood its provisions and were able to make submissions.

He says the timetable appears to have been settled before the people have finished speaking, questioning whether the Committee is genuinely prepared to recommend fundamental changes based on public submissions.

Chand says consultation is not measured by the number of towns visited, meetings conducted or people allowed to speak for five or ten minutes, but by whether people have been given a fair opportunity to understand what is proposed, express their concerns and influence the outcome.

He says the public hearings conducted by the Constitution Review Commission over the past six months cannot be treated as consultations on the Government's Bill, as those hearings sought views on what Fijians wanted in a Constitution and the Bill has ignored salient features of the Commission's report, particularly in terms of separation of powers, transparency and accountability.

Chand says the Government's Bill differs significantly from the draft prepared by the Constitution Review Commission, requiring people who previously made submissions to examine another constitutional text and understand what has changed.

He says the Reeves Commission began its consultations in July 1995 and handed over its report in September 1996, with the 1997 Constitution passed by both Houses of Parliament in July 1997, ten months after the report was handed to the President.

Chand says the current process is a facade and a gross violation of democratic principles.

He says the NFP has identified 18 fundamental constitutional principles that must be addressed, including opposition to the establishment of Christianity as a founding constitutional value of the State, while accepting appropriate recognition of Christianity and other faiths in the Preamble.

He says the party insists upon security for landowners and tenants alike, a 56-member House of Representatives elected through a genuinely proportional mixed-member electoral system, and a Senate that reflects the diversity of Fiji rather than being dominated by one institution.

Chand says the NFP also opposes constitutional immunity for those responsible for political upheavals and provisions permitting the physical chastisement of children, while insisting upon independent constitutional offices, access to justice and effective protection of fundamental rights.

He says the party has consistently called for the removal of the 2013 Constitution because it was imposed upon the people without their consent.

Chand says changing the words of a Constitution means very little if the same disregard for meaningful public participation is repeated.

Chand says even the Fiji Human Rights and Anti-Discrimination Commission has expressed serious concern about the inadequacy of the consultation period.

He says the NFP Management Board has resolved that public consultations must be extended until at least mid-December, with the party's continued participation and support conditional upon a meaningful extension and substantive changes to the Bill.

Chand says there is absolutely no national emergency requiring the Constitution to be rushed through Parliament, adding that the next general elections can proceed under the existing constitutional arrangements while constitutional reform continues with proper public involvement.

He says the NFP will not lend its name to a process that confuses speed with progress or attendance with consent.

item.title: Sayed-Khaiyum urges Rabuka to stop Constitution Amendment Bill

item.content:encoded:
Former Attorney-General Aiyaz Sayed-Khaiyum has urged Prime Minister, Sitiveni RabukaÂ to stop the Constitution Amendment Bill from proceeding to its third reading, saying more time is needed for public consultation and proper examination of the proposed changes.

While making his submission to the Join Parliamentary Selected Committee on the Constitution (Amendment) Bill in Labasa, Sayed-Khaiyum says many people have raised concerns about the limited time available to examine the complex document. Insert:Â Khaiyum on theÂ limited time available 24th Oct 26 PT

He says the drafting contains numerous grammatical errors, incorrect cross-references and ambiguous provisions that need to be reviewed carefully.

Sayed-Khaiyum gives the commencement provisions as an example, saying the Bill contains inconsistencies over when the proposed constitutional amendments would take effect.

He specifically questions Clause 211, which allows the President to bring the amendments into effect earlier through a proclamation published in the Gazette, despite the Bill stating that it would come into force on 31st March 2028.

He argues that this provision conflicts with Section 166 of the 2013 Constitution and says the Bill is fundamentally flawed in this respect.

Sayed-Khaiyum also urges the committee to examine whether the proposed amendments comply with international conventions ratified by Fiji.

He says the Bill of Rights must be strong enough to protect both minority and majority communities, warning against taking an ethnic approach to constitutional reform.

On iTaukei land rights, Sayed-Khaiyum says the 2013 Constitution provides protections for customary land, including provisions relating to compensation when land is acquired for public purposes and the return of land when it is no longer required for that purpose.

He also highlights the constitutional restriction on converting iTaukei land to freehold land, saying concerns about the protection of indigenous land rights should be considered in light of these existing safeguards.

Sayed-Khaiyum says many people view the proposed changes as amounting to a new Constitution rather than amendments to the existing one.

On religion, he argues that the current Constitution already provides for a secular state and protects religious freedom, including the right of faith-based schools to provide religious instruction.

He says the existing provisions require the Government to remain neutral and allow people to practise their own faith.

Sayed-Khaiyum also questions the proposed role of the Bose Levu Vakaturaga, in appointing the President and Vice-President.

He says the President should symbolise the unity of the Republic and represent all Fijians, rather than having the appointment process placed exclusively in the hands of an unelected body.

He also raises concerns that the proposed arrangements could deepen divisions within iTaukei communities, particularly between chiefs, ordinary iTaukei people and those with different levels of wealth and influence.

On the proposed electoral system, Sayed-Khaiyum warns that first-past-the-post voting could result in a candidate winning a constituency despite receiving only a small proportion of the total votes cast.

He gives an example of a constituency with 10,000 voters, where a candidate could win with 1,000 votes while the remaining 9,000 votes are divided among other candidates.

He says this could leave the majority of voters without their preferred representative.

Sayed-Khaiyum also disagrees with the proposal to extend the parliamentary term to five years and questions why certain maritime areas, including Lau, Kadavu, Yasawa, Rotuma and Lomaiviti, would receive special representation compared with other parts of Fiji.

He says more time is needed to examine the proposed changes and urges Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka to stop the Bill from proceeding to its third reading.

Sayed-Khaiyum says the additional time would allow the public to better understand the proposals and give the Government an opportunity to address the concerns raised during consultations.
